text.p: Zimbabwe's long-awaited privatisation programme is expected to gather momentum this year following the announcement on Thursday of the government's first public sale of a state firm, market analysts said.

The equity market and economic analysts said the government's public offer of 75 percent of its stake in the national dairy, Dairibord Zimbabwe Limited (DZL), signalled its seriousness in implementing the programme, which has been on the backburner since the country embarked on market-led economic reforms in 1991.

"Assuming the price is reasonable, we expect the offer to find considerable support and are optimistic that it will signal the long awaited privatisation drive," Dataworld Nominees market and economic analyst Jason Moore said.
The government of President Robert Mugabe has been under pressure from Western donors bankrolling its economic reforms to privatise loss-making firms.

Zimbabwe's budget deficit has averaged over 10 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) since 1991 and is projected at 11.4 percent in the financial year ending June 30 against a target of 8.5 percent.
The government committed to a privatisation programme six years ago but so far has made little progress in implementing it.

"This is arguably the most meaningful move yet in terms of government's attempts at reducing the budget deficit and is potentially excellent news for the economy," Moore told Reuters in reference to the DZL offer.
"The implication is that further privatisations will happen...We are expecting further developments this year," Zimbabwe Stock Exchange (ZSE) chief executive Anthony Barfoot said.
Some brokers said they expected the Cotton Company of Zimbabwe to follow DZL before the end of the year.

"The perception is that the government has now opened the dam wall a little and hopefully the wall will burst and other privatisations will follow hard and fast. The stock exchange fraternity is encouraged," said a broker with Quincor James Capel.

Under the proposed new share structure, the public would hold 15 percent of the shares. A yet-to-be-identified technical partner would have 10 percent, with an option to buy a further 15 percent of the company's equity from a remaining 40 percent stake held by the government.

The state National Investment Trust which was formed to promote the government's programme to economically empower the country's majority blacks, large-scale milk producers and DZL employees would hold 10 percent each. Small-scale producers would have five percent of the company's shares.

The government said a decision to list DZL shares on the Zimbabwe Stock Exchange would rest with the directors of the privatised company. Market analysts said they expected it to be listed in October, boosting scrip on the local bourse. ($1=Z$11.31)
